stem: Explain two limitations of the Gini coefficient as a measure of inequality.

points.description: It is a single figure, so different distributions can have the same Gini.
It does not show where in the distribution the inequality lies.
It does not show the level of income or whether the poor are getting better off.
It depends on how the data are collected (income or wealth, before or after tax, informal incomes).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Gini is a single figure, so different distributions can give the same value and it does not show where in the distribution the inequality lies. It also does not show the level of income or whether the poor are better off, and it depends on how the data are collected, for example whether income is measured before or after tax and whether informal incomes are included.

explanation: Two limitations explained.
hints: Think of what the Gini leaves out.

stem: Assess the usefulness of the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient for comparing inequality between countries.

points.description: The Lorenz curve gives a visual picture of the whole distribution.
The Gini summarises it in a single figure that can be compared across countries and over time.
If one curve lies wholly inside another, the ranking is clear.
Curves can cross and different distributions can have the same Gini.
Neither shows the level of income.
Data differences (income or wealth, before or after tax, household size, informal incomes) reduce comparability.
Other measures (quintile ratios, poverty rates) complement them.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one or both sides, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Lorenz curve gives a visual picture of the whole distribution of income and the Gini summarises it in a single figure which can be compared between countries and over time. If one Lorenz curve lies wholly inside another, the ranking of the two is clear. However, curves can cross and different distributions can have the same Gini, and neither measure shows the level of income, so a poor country and a rich country may have the same Gini. Differences in how the data are collected, for example whether income or wealth is measured, before or after tax, and whether informal incomes are included, also reduce comparability. Other measures such as quintile ratios and poverty rates are therefore needed. Overall the Lorenz curve and Gini are useful for broad comparison but should not be used alone.

explanation: Weigh clarity and comparability against loss of detail and data differences.
hints: Consider what the Lorenz curve and Gini show and what they miss.
